blocks.heading: What this section asks you to do
blocks.text: Define a multinational company, explain why firms operate across borders, and weigh the costs and benefits they bring to a host country and to their home country.
blocks.repair_note: coverage gaps filled from syllabus guidance

blocks.heading: What a multinational company is
blocks.text: A multinational company (MNC) is a firm that produces goods or services in more than one country, through plants, offices or other operations it runs there. A firm that sells abroad from its home base is exporting; it becomes multinational when it produces abroad. The country of its head office is its home country; each other country where it operates is a host country. Most products a learner can name - drinks, phones, clothing - are made and sold this way, and the spread of these firms is one of the engines of globalisation: the same product, sold in many countries, often assembled in several of them.

blocks.heading: A plant opens in Oshakati
blocks.text: Haneda Electronics keeps its head office in Nagoya, Japan, and has opened an assembly plant in Oshakati. The plant pays 300 workers an average of N$6 500 a month, and the 60 technicians it trained now also maintain machinery for other firms in the town. Its profit, about N$12 million a year, is paid to the head office. The host country, Namibia, gains jobs, wages and skills that spread beyond the plant; the home country, Japan, gains profit and a market it did not serve before, though the assembly jobs, and the tax on their wages, went to Namibia rather than to a Japanese town; and the cost that travels with them is that local electronics sellers now face a competitor with far larger resources behind it.

blocks.heading: Costs and benefits to host and home countries
blocks.text:
The Oshakati plant shows the pattern; the full set of costs and benefits runs as follows.

Benefits to the host country. An MNC brings investment the host may not be able to fund from its own saving: buildings, machinery, sometimes roads and power lines. It creates jobs and pays wages, often above what local firms pay. Training and new technology spread to local firms as workers move on, as with the 60 Oshakati technicians. The government collects tax on profits and wages, and where the MNC exports, the host earns foreign currency. Consumers may gain wider choice and lower prices.

Costs to the host country. Profits are usually sent back to the home country, so part of the income created leaves the economy: Haneda's N$12 million a year is income Namibia does not keep. Local firms may be forced out by a competitor with far greater resources. Where rules are weak, wages and working conditions may be poor, and mining or processing may damage the environment or use up natural resources. An MNC is often footloose: if costs rise or a cheaper location appears, it may close the plant and move, leaving workers and suppliers without income. A large MNC may also use its size to press the government for tax breaks or lighter regulation.

Benefits to the home country. Profits sent back from abroad raise the home country's national income and may be taxed there, and shareholders gain. The firm reaches larger markets and cheaper inputs, so it can grow and keep its skilled head-office jobs - design, research, finance - at home.

Costs to the home country. Production jobs, and the investment behind them, move abroad: the assembly work at Oshakati could have been done in a Japanese town. Tax revenue is lost where profits are booked in a lower-tax host, and exports may fall where the foreign plant now supplies a market that home factories once served.

blocks.heading: Multinational is not a kind of ownership
blocks.text: Learners mix up three questions that sound alike. A public limited company sells its shares on a stock exchange - that is ownership traded to the public. A state-owned company belongs to a government - that is who owns it. A multinational company produces in more than one country - that is where it operates. One firm may be any combination of the three: a state-owned airline that flies to and keeps offices in other countries is state-owned and multinational at once. The test: ask which question the sentence answers - ownership traded, who owns it, or where it operates.
